Ours takes thirty-six. That is not us being precious. Long fermentation lets the wild yeast and bacteria break down more of the gluten and starch, which is why a lot of people who struggle with bread find ours easier going. It also gives the crust that deep, slightly sour crackle. We mix on Tuesday morning, shape on Wednesday, and bake through the night. Then it is in your bread bin by breakfast.'], ['Stop putting your bread in the fridge','Baking tips','Here is the single most useful thing we can tell you: the fridge is where bread goes to die. Cold temperatures speed up staling, so a loaf that would have been fine on day three tastes like cardboard on day two. Keep it cut side down on a board, or in a cloth bag. If you will not finish it in three days, slice it and freeze it. Toast straight from frozen. Honestly, it is better than fresh.'], ['Meet Dennis, the starter who runs the place','Behind the scenes','Dennis is five years old, lives in a glass jar on the second shelf, and has never had a day off. He eats rye flour and water twice a day and in return he raises every loaf we sell. People ask if they can buy some of him. You can, actually. We sell little pots of Dennis on Saturdays, with a card telling you how to keep him alive. Most people manage it.'], ['What a 4am bake actually looks like','Behind the scenes','The alarm goes at half three. By four the ovens are hot and the first trays of baguettes go in.
